title: Ὄνος καὶ ὀνηλάτης
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 277. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνος ὑπὸ ὀνηλάτου ἀγόμενος, ὡς μικρὸν τῆς ὁδοῦ προῆλθεν, ἀφεὶς τὴν λείαν ἀτραπὸν διὰ κρημνῶν ἐφέρετο.
sentences.tr: Onos hypo onēlatou agomenos, hōs mikron tēs hodou proēlthen, apheis tēn leian atrapon dia krēmnōn ephereto.
sentences.l: A donkey, being led by a donkey-driver, when he had gone forward a little of the road, having left the smooth track, was rushing along through the crags.
sentences.i: A donkey being led by his driver, once he had gone a little way along the road, left the smooth track and went plunging off through the crags.
sentences.n: μικρὸν τῆς ὁδοῦ is a partitive genitive, 'a little of the road'. ἐφέρετο is the middle-passive of φέρω in its regular sense of a creature or thing rushing headlong — not merely 'was carried'.

sentences.t: Μέλλοντος δὲ αὐτοῦ κατακρημνίζεσθαι, ὁ ὀνηλάτης ἐπιλαβόμενος τῆς οὐρᾶς, ἐπειρᾶτο μεταπεριάγειν αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Mellontos de autou katakrēmnizesthai, ho onēlatēs epilabomenos tēs ouras, epeirato metaperiagein auton.
sentences.l: And when he was about to be flung down the crag, the donkey-driver, having taken hold of his tail, tried to turn him back the other way.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute, Μέλλοντος … αὐτοῦ, the construction the fables run on. ἐπιλαμβάνομαι in the middle takes the genitive of what one lays hold of, τῆς οὐρᾶς.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ εὐτόνως ἀντιπίπτοντος, ἀφεὶς αὐτὸν ἔφη· « Νίκα· κακὴν γὰρ νίκην νικᾷς. »
sentences.tr: Tou de eutonōs antipiptontos, apheis auton ephē· « Nika· kakēn gar nikēn nikāis. »
sentences.l: But as the donkey resisted stoutly, letting him go he said: « Win; for a bad victory you are winning. »
sentences.i: But since the donkey strained stoutly against him, he let him go and said: « Win, then — it is a bad victory you are winning. »
sentences.n: νίκην νικᾷς is a cognate accusative: the noun repeats the verb's own root, a favourite Greek figure that English can only render by keeping both words. ἀντιπίπτω is to fall against, and so to pull the opposite way.

sentences.t: Πρὸς ἄνδρα φιλόνεικον ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros andra philoneikon ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against a contentious man the story is well-timed.
sentences.i: The story is well aimed at the man who must win.
sentences.n: φιλόνεικος as printed is formed on νεῖκος, 'strife', and so means 'contentious'; ancient copies interchange it freely with φιλόνικος, 'fond of victory', and the donkey's closing νίκην νικᾷς pulls the word toward that second sense. The same phrase closes fable 160, where Chambry brackets it as an interpolation; here he prints it plain, with the full εὔκαιρος formula.
